answer: Each head needs cover from an independent underwriter who prices it against its own claims history; policies are written per address and never twice for one owner, so heads that pay out in lockstep get repriced upward and then refused outright. The scarce input is underwriting appetite, which is finite, rationed per head and useless to a sibling, so the second head costs more than the first and the tenth earns less than it pays. A meadow of identical policies is the bridge that betrays the cluster, and one correlated claim ripples through every book the owner opens.
